summary: This informational document analyzes how hashes are used in Secure Neighbor Discovery and how attacks on hash functions affect it. SEND uses SHA-1 and has no hash agility, so the document assesses the risk.

eli5.summary: A security system for neighbor lookup relies on a fingerprint machine that has cracks. This studies how risky that is.

questions: is secure neighbor discovery safe from sha-1 attacks
what hash functions does send use
is send vulnerable to sha-1 attacks
why are collision attacks less dangerous than preimage attacks
subtitle: Evaluating hash function vulnerabilities in secure neighbor discovery.

tldr.problem: Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) relies on the SHA-1 hash algorithm to bind cryptographic keys to IPv6 addresses, but collision attacks have been demonstrated against SHA-1 and other widely used hashes.
tldr.mechanism: The document analyzes where SEND uses hashes—in cryptographically generated addresses (CGAs), digital signatures, and X.509 certificates—and assesses whether known hash attacks actually pose a practical threat.
tldr.outcome: Most hash attacks do not threaten SEND's security, except through attacks on the CGA mechanism itself, which the authors recommend addressing by encoding hash algorithm information into CGAs.

facts.label: Hash algorithm
facts.value: SHA-1 in SEND; MD5 in some X.509 certificates

today: RFC 6273 is Informational and documents the threat analysis as of 2011. SEND itself remains defined by RFC 3971, and hash-agile CGA support is specified in RFC 4982. The security community's assessment of hash function strength has evolved, particularly regarding SHA-1, validating the document's focus on the need for algorithm agility.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SEND (Secure Neighbor Discovery) is an IPv6 security protocol that uses the SHA-1 hash algorithm to associate cryptographic keys with IPv6 addresses and to create digital signatures on router authorization certificates. The document was written when researchers had recently demonstrated collision attacks against SHA-1 and similar attacks against MD5 used in X.509 certificates.

The authors set out to determine whether these cryptographic attacks pose a real threat to SEND's actual use in networks. Rather than assume the worst, they analyze each place where SEND uses hashing and evaluate the practical impact of each type of attack.
sections.eli5: People found ways to break SHA-1 fingerprints. The document checks if those breaks can actually hurt SEND.

sections.title: How SEND Uses Hashes
sections.content:
SEND relies on hashes in four distinct places. First, it uses SHA-1 in Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs), which bind a public key to an IPv6 address by hashing the key material. Second, it hashes key material again in the Key Hash field of the RSA Signature option. Third, SEND uses hashes embedded in X.509 certificates from a trust anchor to authorize routers. Fourth, it uses SHA-1 to create digital signatures over neighbor discovery messages.

Each of these uses has different properties. Some rely on the collision-resistance of the hash—its ability to resist finding two different inputs that produce the same output. Others rely on preimage resistance—the difficulty of finding any input that hashes to a target value. Understanding which property matters for each use is key to assessing risk.
sections.eli5: SEND checks fingerprints in four different places: when making addresses, when signing messages, when checking router certificates, and when protecting key material. Each place needs a different kind of protection.

sections.title: Threat Analysis
sections.content:
Attacks on CGAs present the most significant risk. CGAs do not depend on collision resistance—an attacker cannot forge a CGA by finding a collision. However, if preimage attacks become practical (finding any key material that hashes to a target address), an attacker could generate a new CGA that appears to belong to a victim. This is the only attack the document identifies as genuinely dangerous to SEND's operation.

Attacks on digital signatures and key hashes are analyzed as not practically exploitable. Collision attacks on the SHA-1 signature itself cannot work because the structure of neighbor discovery messages is rigid and well-known; an attacker cannot create two different meaningful messages with the same hash. Attacks on the Key Hash field also fail because the real key is already authorized through separate mechanisms (either the CGA itself or router certificates), so any hash collision would be detected immediately as invalid.

Attacks on X.509 certificates using MD5 could theoretically allow an attacker to create a forged router certificate with a different identity if they can predict unpredictable fields like serial numbers and validity periods. In practice, the certificate authority can detect such forgeries if necessary, limiting the window of exposure.
sections.eli5: Breaking fingerprints in messages is hard because messages have a fixed shape. Breaking fingerprints on certificates is possible in theory but hard in practice because the CA can spot the fake.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The analysis concludes that current hash function attacks, while impressive as cryptographic research, do not constitute a practical threat to most of SEND's mechanisms. The digital signatures in SEND messages, the key hashes they contain, and even the X.509 certificates used for router authorization all remain secure against known attacks.

The one exception is the CGA mechanism: if preimage attacks on SHA-1 become feasible, SEND would be compromised. To mitigate this risk, the authors recommend that CGAs encode the hash algorithm used during generation, allowing the system to migrate to stronger hashes without breaking compatibility. This approach, specified separately in RFC 4982, lets SEND remain secure even if SHA-1 weakens further.
sections.eli5: Most of SEND is safe. Only the address fingerprints are at risk, and that risk can be managed by letting the system remember which fingerprint machine was used.
